title: Vessel walls: arteries, veins and plaque
summary: The three tunics, elastic versus muscular arteries, how to tell artery, vein and nerve apart, and arteriosclerosis.
objectives: Name the three tunics and the tissues in each
Contrast elastic and muscular arteries, and arteries with veins
Identify an artery, a vein and a nerve in cross-section
Describe where an arteriosclerotic plaque forms and its effects
takeaways: Intima (endothelium + basement membrane + thin connective tissue), media (smooth muscle ± elastic), externa (connective tissue with vasa vasorum and nerves).
Arteries have internal and external elastic membranes and a thick media; veins have a thin media, wide lumen and often valves.
Elastic (conducting) arteries near the heart stretch and recoil; muscular (distributing) arteries control distribution.
Plaque forms deep to the endothelium in the intima, narrowing the lumen and stiffening the wall.

steps.title: Three tunics
steps.text: Arteries and veins share three layers. The tunica intima (interna) is the endothelium - simple squamous cells in contact with the blood - on a basement membrane and a thin layer of connective tissue (lamina propria). The tunica media is circular smooth muscle, with elastic fibres in arteries. The tunica externa (adventitia) is a connective-tissue sheath anchoring the vessel.

check.q: Which layer of a vessel is in contact with the blood?
check.a: The endothelium of the tunica intima.

steps.title: Elastic membranes, vessels and nerves of the wall
steps.text:
In arteries a wavy internal elastic membrane separates intima from media, and an external elastic membrane separates media from externa.

Thick walls cannot be fed from the lumen alone, so large vessels have their own small vessels, the vasa vasorum, in the externa. Nerves there (nervi vasorum) control the smooth muscle and so the vessel's diameter.

check.q: What are the vasa vasorum?
check.a: Small blood vessels supplying the wall of a large vessel.

steps.title: Elastic and muscular arteries
steps.text:
Near the heart are elastic (conducting) arteries - the aorta and its largest branches - whose media is packed with elastic lamellae. They stretch as the ventricle ejects and recoil in diastole, keeping blood moving.

Farther out, the media becomes mostly smooth muscle: muscular (distributing) arteries such as the brachial or femoral, which adjust how much blood each region receives. The change is gradual.

check.q: Why is the aorta an elastic artery?
check.a: Its elastic media stretches in systole and recoils in diastole, smoothing and maintaining flow.

steps.title: Veins, and telling vessels apart
steps.text:
Veins carry blood at low pressure. Their media is thin, the externa relatively thick and the lumen wide and often collapsed. Many limb veins have valves - folds of the intima - that stop backflow; arteries have none.

In a slide, an artery has a thick media, round lumen and wavy intima; a vein a thin wall and large, irregular lumen; a nerve is solid, filled with bundles of fibres.

check.q: How do you tell a nerve from a vessel in cross-section?
check.a: A nerve is solid, packed with fascicles of fibres; a vessel has a lumen.

steps.title: Arteriosclerosis
steps.text:
Arteriosclerosis - 'hardening of the arteries' - is loss of elasticity and thickening of the artery wall. In its commonest form a cholesterol plaque builds up deep to the endothelium, in the intima.

The plaque narrows the lumen and cuts flow, and a rough or ruptured plaque can trigger a thrombus that blocks the vessel. In the coronary arteries this is coronary artery disease.

check.q: In which tunic does an atherosclerotic plaque form?
check.a: In the tunica intima, deep to the endothelium.

practice.q: Order the layers of an artery wall from the lumen outward
Which feature identifies a vein in section?
practice.why: Veins have thin walls and large, often collapsed lumens.

practice.q: Muscular (distributing) arteries differ from elastic arteries by having:
choices: More smooth muscle in the media
practice.why: Their media is mostly smooth muscle, to regulate distribution.

practice.q: Arteriosclerotic plaque develops:
choices: Deep to the endothelium in the intima
practice.why: The plaque builds up in the intima beneath the endothelium.

practice.q: Name two consequences of arteriosclerosis.
practice.a: Narrowed lumen with reduced flow; loss of elasticity; thrombus formation (e.g. coronary artery disease).

practice.q: What does the tunica intima consist of?
practice.a: Endothelium (simple squamous epithelium), basement membrane and a thin connective-tissue layer.

practice.q: What do 'a.' and 'aa.' mean on a labelled figure?
practice.a: Artery and arteries (v. and vv. for vein and veins).

practice.q: What controls the diameter of an artery?
practice.a: Smooth muscle of the tunica media, under the control of nerves in the externa.

title: The aorta and its branches in the chest
summary: Ascending aorta, arch and descending aorta, and the branches each gives off.
objectives: Name the parts of the aorta
List the three branches of the aortic arch and the division of the brachiocephalic trunk
Name the branches of the thoracic aorta and the internal thoracic artery
takeaways: Ascending aorta → coronary arteries; arch → brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian.
Brachiocephalic trunk (right only) → right common carotid + right subclavian.
Descending aorta = thoracic (above diaphragm) + abdominal (below).
Thoracic aorta → posterior intercostal, oesophageal, bronchial, superior phrenic; internal thoracic → anterior intercostals.

steps.title: Ascending aorta and arch
steps.text: The aorta leaves the left ventricle as the thick-walled ascending aorta, which carries the highest pressure in the body; its only branches are the coronary arteries. It curves up and back to the left as the aortic arch, which gives three branches: the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid and the left subclavian artery.

check.q: Name the three branches of the aortic arch from right to left.
check.a: Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, left subclavian artery.

steps.title: The brachiocephalic trunk
steps.text:
There is a brachiocephalic trunk only on the right. It runs up behind the right sternoclavicular joint and divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.

So the right common carotid and subclavian are second-generation branches, while their left-sided partners come straight off the arch.

check.q: What are the two branches of the brachiocephalic trunk?
check.a: The right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.

steps.title: The descending aorta
steps.text:
After the arch the descending aorta runs down beside the vertebral bodies. Above the diaphragm it is the thoracic aorta; after passing through the diaphragm it is the abdominal aorta.

The thoracic aorta gives paired posterior intercostal arteries to the intercostal spaces, small visceral branches to the oesophagus and bronchi, and superior phrenic arteries to the top of the diaphragm.

check.q: Where does the thoracic aorta become the abdominal aorta?
check.a: Where it passes through the diaphragm (aortic hiatus, T12).

steps.title: The internal thoracic artery
steps.text:
The internal thoracic artery is a branch of the subclavian. It runs down just behind the costal cartilages, a finger's breadth from the edge of the sternum, and gives anterior intercostal arteries into each space.

These meet the posterior intercostals from the aorta, so every intercostal space has a ring of arteries fed from both ends - an anastomosis.

check.q: What does the internal thoracic artery supply to the intercostal spaces?
check.a: The anterior intercostal arteries.

practice.q: Order the branches of the aortic arch from right to left
The first branches of the aorta are the:
practice.why: The coronary arteries arise from the ascending aorta.

practice.q: Which artery gives the anterior intercostal arteries?
practice.why: The internal thoracic (a subclavian branch) supplies them.

practice.q: Name the visceral branches of the thoracic aorta.
practice.a: Oesophageal and bronchial arteries (also superior phrenic to the diaphragm).

title: Arteries of the head and neck
summary: The common carotid and its two divisions, the branches of the external carotid, and the vertebral artery.
objectives: Describe the course and bifurcation of the common carotid artery
List the branches of the external carotid artery
Trace the internal carotid and vertebral arteries into the skull
takeaways: The common carotid divides at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, just below the angle of the jaw.
Carotid sinus: baroreceptor dilation at the origin of the internal carotid.
Internal carotid: no neck branches, enters via the carotid canal to the brain.
External carotid: superior thyroid, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, maxillary, superficial temporal. Vertebral: transverse foramina → foramen magnum.

steps.title: The common carotid and its fork
steps.text:
The common carotid artery runs up the neck beside the trachea and larynx - left from the arch, right from the brachiocephalic trunk. At the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, just below the angle of the mandible, it divides into the internal and external carotid arteries.

The carotid pulse is felt here, in front of the sternocleidomastoid.

check.q: At what level does the common carotid divide?
check.a: At the upper border of the thyroid cartilage, just below the angle of the mandible.

steps.title: Internal carotid and carotid sinus
steps.text:
At its origin the internal carotid is slightly dilated: the carotid sinus, whose wall holds baroreceptors that sense blood pressure.

The internal carotid gives no branches in the neck. It enters the skull through the carotid canal of the temporal bone and supplies most of the cerebrum and the eye.

check.q: What is the carotid sinus?
check.a: A dilation at the origin of the internal carotid artery containing baroreceptors.

steps.title: Branches of the external carotid
steps.text: The external carotid supplies the neck, face and scalp. Its branches are the superior thyroid (thyroid, larynx), lingual (tongue), facial (face), occipital (back of scalp), posterior auricular (behind the ear), and its two terminal branches, the maxillary (jaws, deep face) and superficial temporal (side of the scalp).
steps.mnemonic: Some Lovers Find Oddly Peculiar Moments Special: Superior thyroid, Lingual, Facial, Occipital, Posterior auricular, Maxillary, Superficial temporal.

check.q: What are the two terminal branches of the external carotid?
check.a: The maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.

steps.title: The vertebral artery
steps.text: The vertebral artery arises from the subclavian, climbs through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae (C6 up to C1), and enters the skull through the foramen magnum. There the two vertebral arteries join on the front of the brainstem to form the basilar artery.

check.q: Through which openings does the vertebral artery pass?
check.a: The transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae, then the foramen magnum.

practice.q: List the external carotid branches from below upward
Which carotid branch has no branches in the neck?
practice.why: The internal carotid runs straight to the carotid canal.

practice.q: The internal carotid enters the skull through the:
practice.why: The carotid canal of the temporal bone.

practice.q: Which external carotid branches supply the tongue and the thyroid gland?

title: Blood supply to the brain: the circle of Willis
summary: Four arteries in, one ring at the base of the brain, and the cerebral and cerebellar arteries it feeds.
objectives: Name the four arteries that supply the brain
List the components of the cerebral arterial circle
Name the cerebral, cerebellar and spinal arteries and explain collateral circulation
takeaways: Brain: two internal carotids + two vertebrals (→ basilar).
Circle: anterior communicating, anterior cerebrals, internal carotids, posterior communicatings, posterior cerebrals - around the pituitary and optic chiasm.
Anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries supply the cerebrum; superior, anterior inferior and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries the cerebellum.
Anastomoses give collateral routes if one artery is blocked.

steps.title: Four arteries in
steps.text:
The brain receives all its blood through four arteries: the two internal carotids in front and the two vertebral arteries behind. The vertebrals unite on the pons as the basilar artery.

The arteries and their branches run over the brain's surface in the subarachnoid space, sending fine branches inward, rather than tunnelling deep through the tissue.

check.q: Which four arteries supply the brain?
check.a: The right and left internal carotid and right and left vertebral arteries.

steps.title: The circle
steps.text: At the base of the brain, around the pituitary gland and optic chiasm, these arteries are joined into a ring, the cerebral arterial circle (circle of Willis). Going round it: the anterior communicating artery, the two anterior cerebral arteries, the ends of the internal carotids, the posterior communicating arteries and the two posterior cerebral arteries from the basilar.

check.q: Which structure sits in the middle of the circle of Willis?
check.a: The pituitary gland (with the optic chiasm in front).

steps.title: Cerebral, cerebellar and spinal arteries
steps.text:
The anterior cerebral supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes, the middle cerebral - the continuation of the internal carotid - most of the lateral surface, and the posterior cerebral the occipital lobe and underside of the temporal lobe.

The superior and anterior inferior cerebellar arteries come from the basilar, the posterior inferior cerebellar from the vertebral; the vertebrals also form the anterior spinal artery.

check.q: Which cerebellar artery arises from the vertebral rather than the basilar artery?
check.a: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery.

steps.title: Collateral circulation
steps.text:
An anastomosis is a joining of vessels that gives blood more than one route. The circle of Willis is the classic example: if one internal carotid or vertebral narrows slowly, blood can still reach its territory from the other side or from behind - collateral circulation.

The circle is often incomplete, and a sudden blockage of a single cerebral artery beyond the ring still causes a stroke.

check.q: What is collateral circulation?
check.a: An alternative route for blood through anastomoses when one artery is blocked.

practice.q: Go round the circle of Willis from front to back on one side
The basilar artery is formed by:
practice.why: The vertebral arteries unite on the pons.

practice.q: Which artery is NOT part of the circle of Willis?
practice.why: The middle cerebral leaves the circle laterally; it is not one of the ring's links.

title: Arteries of the upper limb
summary: One artery with changing names from neck to fingers, its branches and its pulse points.
objectives: Trace the arterial supply from subclavian to digital arteries
Name the branches of the subclavian and axillary arteries
Locate the brachial and radial pulses
takeaways: Subclavian → axillary (lateral border of 1st rib) → brachial (lower border of teres major) → radial + ulnar → palmar arches → digital arteries.
Subclavian: vertebral, thyrocervical trunk, internal thoracic, costocervical trunk.
Axillary: thoraco-acromial, lateral thoracic, subscapular, anterior and posterior circumflex humeral.
Brachial pulse medial to biceps (blood-pressure site); radial pulse lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon.

steps.title: The subclavian artery
steps.text:
The subclavian artery (right from the brachiocephalic trunk, left from the arch) arches over the first rib. Its branches are the vertebral artery, the thyrocervical trunk (thyroid, neck, shoulder), the internal thoracic artery (front of the chest wall) and the costocervical trunk (deep neck, first intercostal spaces).

At the lateral border of the first rib it becomes the axillary artery.

check.q: Where does the subclavian artery become the axillary artery?
check.a: At the lateral border of the first rib.

steps.title: The axillary artery
steps.text: The axillary artery runs through the armpit to the lower border of teres major. It supplies the shoulder, chest wall and upper back: the thoraco-acromial artery (pectoral muscles, shoulder), the lateral thoracic (side of the chest), the subscapular (scapular muscles, latissimus dorsi) and the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries around the surgical neck of the humerus.

check.q: Name the branch that winds behind the surgical neck of the humerus.
check.a: The posterior circumflex humeral artery.

steps.title: The brachial artery
steps.text:
Beyond teres major the vessel is the brachial artery, running down the medial arm. Its deep brachial branch spirals behind the humerus to supply the triceps brachii and the bone.

The brachial pulse is felt in the groove on the medial side of the lower arm, between biceps brachii and brachialis, just above the elbow - where the stethoscope goes for a blood-pressure reading.

check.q: Which muscle does the deep brachial artery mainly supply?
check.a: Triceps brachii.

steps.title: Radial and ulnar arteries
steps.text:
Just below the elbow the brachial artery divides into the radial artery, down the lateral forearm, and the ulnar artery, down the medial forearm.

At the wrist the radial artery lies just lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis, where the radial pulse is taken.

check.q: Where is the radial pulse felt?
check.a: At the wrist, just lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon.

steps.title: Palmar arches and digital arteries
steps.text:
In the hand the radial and ulnar arteries anastomose to form two arches: the superficial palmar arch (mainly ulnar) and the deep palmar arch (mainly radial). From the arches, digital arteries run along the fingers.

Because of the arches, a hand survives if either radial or ulnar artery is blocked.

check.q: Which two arteries form the palmar arches?
check.a: The radial and ulnar arteries.

practice.q: Trace arterial blood from the arch to the fingers
The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the:
practice.why: It changes name at the lower border of teres major.

practice.q: Where is the stethoscope placed to measure blood pressure in the arm?
practice.a: Over the brachial artery, medial to the biceps tendon just above the elbow.

title: The abdominal aorta and its branches
summary: From the diaphragm to the bifurcation: the gut arteries and the paired branches, in order.
objectives: List the branches of the abdominal aorta from top to bottom
Name the branches and territories of the coeliac trunk and the mesenteric arteries
Distinguish the unpaired visceral branches from the paired branches
takeaways: Order: inferior phrenic, coeliac, superior mesenteric, middle suprarenal, renal, gonadal, lumbar, inferior mesenteric, median sacral, then common iliacs (L4).
Coeliac trunk → left gastric, splenic, common hepatic.
SMA → jejunal and ileal, ileocolic, right colic, middle colic: small intestine to mid transverse colon.
IMA → distal transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, upper rectum.

steps.title: Branches in order
steps.text:
The abdominal aorta runs from the diaphragm (T12) to its bifurcation at L4. From top to bottom it gives: inferior phrenic, coeliac trunk, superior mesenteric, middle suprarenal, renal, gonadal, lumbar, inferior mesenteric and median sacral arteries, then divides into the common iliacs.

The three gut arteries are unpaired; the rest, except the median sacral, are paired.

check.q: Name the three unpaired arteries to the gut.
check.a: Coeliac trunk, superior mesenteric artery and inferior mesenteric artery.

steps.title: The coeliac trunk
steps.text: Just below the diaphragm the short coeliac trunk splits three ways: the left gastric artery to the stomach and lower oesophagus; the splenic artery, running left along the pancreas to the spleen, pancreas and stomach; and the common hepatic artery to the liver, gallbladder, stomach and duodenum.

check.q: What are the three branches of the coeliac trunk?
check.a: Left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries.

steps.title: The superior mesenteric artery
steps.text:
The superior mesenteric artery leaves the aorta about 1 cm lower and runs down in the mesentery. It supplies the small intestine - jejunum and ileum - with the caecum and appendix, ascending colon and most of the transverse colon.

Its branches: many intestinal (jejunal and ileal) arteries to the left, and the ileocolic, right colic and middle colic arteries to the right.

check.q: Which artery supplies the ascending colon?
check.a: The superior mesenteric artery (via ileocolic and right colic branches).

steps.title: The paired branches
steps.text: The paired branches go to the body wall and to the paired organs: inferior phrenic arteries to the underside of the diaphragm, suprarenal arteries to the adrenal glands, renal arteries to the kidneys, gonadal (testicular or ovarian) arteries - which arise just below the renals and run down to the gonads - and four pairs of lumbar arteries to the back and abdominal wall.

check.q: Where do the gonadal arteries arise?
check.a: From the aorta just below the renal arteries.

steps.title: Inferior mesenteric and median sacral
steps.text:
The inferior mesenteric artery (about L3) supplies the distal transverse colon, the descending colon, the sigmoid colon and the upper rectum through its left colic, sigmoid and superior rectal branches.

Finally a slender median sacral artery leaves the back of the bifurcation and runs down the front of the sacrum and coccyx.

check.q: Which part of the colon does the inferior mesenteric artery supply?
check.a: The distal transverse, descending and sigmoid colon (and upper rectum).

practice.q: Put the abdominal aortic branches in order from top to bottom
Which is a paired branch of the abdominal aorta?
practice.why: Renal, suprarenal, gonadal, lumbar and inferior phrenic are paired.

practice.q: The splenic artery is a branch of the:
practice.why: The coeliac trunk.

title: Arteries of the pelvis and lower limb
summary: From the aortic bifurcation to the toes: iliac, femoral, popliteal, tibial and foot arteries.
objectives: Describe the division of the common iliac artery and the territory of each iliac
Name the internal iliac branches shown
Trace the lower-limb arteries to the toes and locate the pulses
takeaways: Aorta → common iliacs (L4) → internal iliac (pelvis) + external iliac (limb).
Internal iliac: lateral sacral, internal pudendal, obturator, superior gluteal.
External iliac → femoral (under inguinal ligament) → popliteal → anterior tibial (→ dorsalis pedis) + posterior tibial (→ fibular, plantar arteries).
Deep femoral → lateral circumflex femoral (with descending branch); genicular arteries round the knee.

steps.title: Common, internal and external iliac
steps.text: At about L4 the aorta divides into the right and left common iliac arteries. In front of the sacroiliac joint each divides into an internal iliac artery, which dives into the pelvis, and an external iliac artery, which follows the pelvic brim toward the thigh and also supplies the lower anterior abdominal wall.

check.q: What are the two divisions of the common iliac artery?
check.a: The internal iliac (pelvis) and external iliac (lower limb).

steps.title: The internal iliac artery
steps.text: The internal iliac supplies the pelvic walls and organs - bladder, rectum, and in women the uterus, vagina and ovary - the pelvic floor, the external genitalia and the gluteal and hip muscles. Branches to know: the lateral sacral arteries (sacrum), the internal pudendal (perineum and genitalia), the obturator (medial thigh) and the superior gluteal (gluteal muscles).

check.q: Which internal iliac branch supplies the external genitalia?
check.a: The internal pudendal.

steps.title: Femoral and deep femoral
steps.text: The external iliac passes under the inguinal ligament, beside the inguinal canal, and becomes the femoral artery, whose pulse is felt in the groin. The femoral supplies the thigh; its large deep femoral branch feeds the thigh muscles, femur and knee. From the deep femoral the lateral circumflex femoral artery sends a long descending branch down the lateral thigh.
focus: Descending branch of lateral circumflex femoral artery

check.q: Where does the external iliac artery become the femoral artery?
check.a: As it passes under the inguinal ligament.

steps.title: Popliteal artery and the leg
steps.text: Behind the knee the femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery (popliteal pulse), which gives genicular arteries round the knee joint. It then divides into the anterior tibial artery, which pierces forward to the anterior leg, and the posterior tibial artery in the back of the leg. The posterior tibial gives the fibular (peroneal) artery to the lateral leg.

check.q: From which artery does the fibular artery arise?
check.a: The posterior tibial artery.

steps.title: Arteries of the foot
steps.text: The anterior tibial crosses the ankle to become the dorsalis pedis artery on the top of the foot, where its pulse is felt. The posterior tibial passes behind the medial malleolus and divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries in the sole; the lateral plantar forms the plantar arch with the dorsalis pedis. Digital arteries run to the toes.

check.q: What does the anterior tibial artery become on the dorsum of the foot?
check.a: The dorsalis pedis artery.

practice.q: Trace arterial blood from the external iliac to the toes on the dorsum of the foot

title: Veins of the head and neck
summary: The dural venous sinuses, the jugular veins and how head and neck blood reaches the superior vena cava.
objectives: Trace blood from the brain through the dural sinuses to the internal jugular vein
Name the tributaries of the internal and external jugular veins
Describe the formation of the brachiocephalic veins and superior vena cava
takeaways: Cerebral veins → dural sinuses: superior and inferior sagittal, straight, transverse, sigmoid, occipital, cavernous, superior and inferior petrosal.
Sigmoid sinus → internal jugular vein at the jugular foramen.
Internal jugular receives facial, lingual, superior thyroid; external jugular (scalp and face) → subclavian.
Internal jugular + subclavian = brachiocephalic; two brachiocephalics = superior vena cava.

steps.title: The dural venous sinuses
steps.text: Veins from the brain cross the subarachnoid and subdural spaces and empty into dural venous sinuses - channels between layers of the dura. The superior sagittal sinus runs along the top of the falx; the inferior sagittal along its free edge drains into the straight sinus. These meet at the back of the skull with the small occipital sinus, then flow out along each transverse and sigmoid sinus.

check.q: Where does the inferior sagittal sinus drain?
check.a: Into the straight sinus.

steps.title: Cavernous and petrosal sinuses
steps.text:
On each side of the pituitary lies a cavernous sinus. It receives the ophthalmic veins from the orbit and drains backward through the superior petrosal sinus (to the transverse/sigmoid) and the inferior petrosal sinus (to the internal jugular).

Because the face and orbit drain here too, an infection near the nose can spread into the cranial cavity.

check.q: Which veins drain the orbit into the cavernous sinus?
check.a: The ophthalmic veins.

steps.title: The internal jugular vein
steps.text:
The sigmoid sinus leaves the skull through the jugular foramen as the internal jugular vein, which runs down the neck beside the common carotid artery. It collects the facial, lingual and superior thyroid veins.

Behind the clavicle it joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.

check.q: Through which opening does blood leave the skull to enter the internal jugular vein?
check.a: The jugular foramen.

steps.title: Superficial veins and the vertebral vein
steps.text:
The scalp and side of the face drain through the superficial temporal veins into the retromandibular vein behind the jaw. The external jugular vein forms near the angle of the mandible, crosses the sternocleidomastoid under the skin and empties into the subclavian vein.

Deep in the neck, vertebral veins descend through the transverse foramina to the brachiocephalic vein.

check.q: Into which vein does the external jugular vein empty?
check.a: The subclavian vein.

steps.title: Brachiocephalic veins and the superior vena cava
steps.text:
On each side the internal jugular and subclavian veins join to form a brachiocephalic vein, which also receives the vertebral and internal thoracic veins. The left brachiocephalic is longer and crosses behind the manubrium.

The two unite to form the superior vena cava, which enters the right atrium.

check.q: Which two veins form each brachiocephalic vein?
check.a: The internal jugular and subclavian veins.

practice.q: Trace blood from the top of the brain to the heart

title: Veins of the upper and lower limbs
summary: Superficial and deep limb veins, the venipuncture site, and the route from toes to inferior vena cava.
objectives: Distinguish superficial from deep veins and explain the role of valves
Trace the veins of the upper limb to the subclavian vein
Trace the veins of the lower limb to the inferior vena cava
takeaways: Deep veins travel with, and are named after, the arteries (often paired); superficial veins run alone.
Cephalic (lateral), basilic (medial), median cubital (venipuncture) and median antebrachial veins.
Brachial + basilic → axillary; axillary + cephalic → subclavian.
Great saphenous (longest, medial, → femoral); small saphenous (→ popliteal); tibials → popliteal → femoral → external iliac → common iliac → IVC.

steps.title: Superficial, deep and valved
steps.text:
Limb veins come in two sets. Deep veins run with the arteries and share their names, often as a pair either side of the artery. Superficial veins run in the subcutaneous tissue with no companion artery, and anastomose freely with each other.

Venous pressure is low, so valves - most numerous in the legs - stop blood falling back, and contracting muscles squeeze it upward against gravity.

check.q: Why do leg veins have many valves?
check.a: Venous pressure is low, and valves prevent backflow against gravity.

steps.title: Superficial veins of the upper limb
steps.text:
Digital veins drain into venous networks and arches of the hand. From these the cephalic vein climbs the lateral (thumb) side of the limb and the basilic vein the medial side; the median antebrachial vein runs up the front of the forearm.

In front of the elbow the median cubital vein crosses the cubital fossa from cephalic to basilic - the usual site for drawing blood.

check.q: Which vein is usually used for venipuncture?
check.a: The median cubital vein in the cubital fossa.

steps.title: Deep veins of the upper limb
steps.text:
Deep digital veins feed the superficial and deep venous palmar arches, which drain into paired radial and ulnar veins; these join as the brachial veins.

The brachial veins and the basilic vein form the axillary vein; the axillary receives the cephalic vein and, at the first rib, becomes the subclavian vein - then brachiocephalic vein and superior vena cava.

check.q: Which two veins join to form the axillary vein?
check.a: The brachial veins and the basilic vein.

steps.title: Superficial veins of the lower limb
steps.text: Digital veins of the toes drain into the dorsal venous arch on the top of the foot. From its medial end the great saphenous vein - the longest vein in the body - passes in front of the medial malleolus, up the medial leg and thigh, and joins the femoral vein in the groin. From the lateral end the small saphenous vein runs behind the lateral malleolus and up the calf to the popliteal vein.

check.q: Where does the great saphenous vein begin and end?
check.a: From the dorsal venous arch, in front of the medial malleolus, to the femoral vein in the groin.

steps.title: Deep veins of the lower limb to the IVC
steps.text: The plantar venous arch drains into the posterior tibial veins, which receive the fibular veins; the anterior tibial veins come from the dorsum. Behind the knee the tibial veins unite as the popliteal vein, which becomes the femoral vein (joined by the deep femoral vein). Under the inguinal ligament it becomes the external iliac vein; with the internal iliac it forms the common iliac, and the two common iliacs form the IVC.

check.q: Which vein does the small saphenous vein drain into?
check.a: The popliteal vein.

practice.q: Trace blood from the sole of the foot to the inferior vena cava
Paired deep veins accompanying an artery are called:
practice.why: Venae comitantes travel either side of the artery.

title: The venae cavae and the azygos system
summary: What drains into the inferior vena cava, the left-sided detour through the renal vein, and the azygos veins of the chest wall.
objectives: List the direct tributaries of the inferior vena cava
Explain why the left gonadal and suprarenal veins drain differently from the right
Describe the azygos, hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins
takeaways: IVC tributaries: common iliacs, lumbar, right gonadal, renal, right suprarenal, inferior phrenic, hepatic.
Left gonadal and left suprarenal veins → left renal vein → IVC.
Posterior intercostal veins → azygos (right) or hemiazygos/accessory hemiazygos (left) → azygos → SVC.
SVC (head, arms, chest wall), IVC (below diaphragm) and coronary sinus (heart) all enter the right atrium.

steps.title: The inferior vena cava
steps.text: Veins joining a larger vein are its tributaries. The two common iliac veins join at about L5, to the right of the aorta, to form the inferior vena cava. As it climbs it receives lumbar veins, the right gonadal vein, both renal veins, the right suprarenal and inferior phrenic veins, and just below the diaphragm the hepatic veins. It passes through the diaphragm into the right atrium.

check.q: Name four direct tributaries of the IVC.
check.a: Any four of: common iliac, lumbar, right gonadal, renal, right suprarenal, inferior phrenic, hepatic veins.

steps.title: The left-sided detour
steps.text:
The IVC lies to the right, so some left-sided veins reach it indirectly. The left gonadal vein and the left suprarenal vein drain into the left renal vein, which then crosses in front of the aorta to the IVC.

On the right, the gonadal and suprarenal veins enter the IVC directly.

check.q: Where does the left gonadal vein drain?
check.a: Into the left renal vein.

steps.title: The azygos system
steps.text: The chest wall drains through posterior intercostal veins. On the right they join the azygos vein, which climbs beside the vertebral bodies and arches forward over the root of the right lung into the superior vena cava. On the left they drain into the hemiazygos (lower) and accessory hemiazygos (upper) veins, which cross to the azygos. Ascending lumbar veins link the lumbar veins to this system.

check.q: Where does the azygos vein end?
check.a: In the superior vena cava.

steps.title: Everything returns to the right atrium
steps.text: Three vessels bring systemic blood home. The superior vena cava drains the head, neck, upper limbs and chest wall (via the brachiocephalic and azygos veins). The inferior vena cava drains everything below the diaphragm - gut blood only after it has passed through the liver. The coronary sinus drains the heart wall itself.

check.q: Which three vessels open into the right atrium?
check.a: Superior vena cava, inferior vena cava and coronary sinus.

practice.q: The left suprarenal vein usually drains into the:
practice.why: Like the left gonadal vein, it joins the left renal vein.

practice.q: Which vein drains the right posterior intercostal veins?
practice.why: The azygos vein, which ends in the SVC.

practice.q: Trace blood from a lower left intercostal space to the heart

title: The hepatic portal system
summary: Why blood from the gut visits the liver before the heart, and the veins that take it there.
objectives: Define a portal system
Name the tributaries that form the hepatic portal vein
Trace blood from the intestine through the liver to the inferior vena cava
takeaways: Portal system: capillary bed → vein → second capillary bed.
Inferior mesenteric → splenic; splenic + superior mesenteric → hepatic portal vein; gastric, gastro-omental and cystic veins join too.
In the liver, sinusoids let hepatocytes store nutrients and Kupffer cells clean the blood.
Sinusoids → central veins → hepatic veins → IVC.

steps.title: A second capillary bed
steps.text: Most blood passes through one capillary bed on each circuit. In a portal system a capillary bed drains into a vein that feeds a second capillary bed. Blood from the stomach, intestines, pancreas and spleen goes first to the liver sinusoids. There hepatocytes take up and store nutrients and remove toxins, and Kupffer cells (macrophages) remove bacteria and debris.

check.q: What is a portal system?
check.a: A capillary bed draining through a vein into a second capillary bed.

steps.title: The tributaries
steps.text: The inferior mesenteric vein (distal large intestine) usually joins the splenic vein, which runs behind the pancreas collecting pancreatic veins. Behind the neck of the pancreas the splenic vein meets the superior mesenteric vein (small intestine and proximal colon) to form the hepatic portal vein. The gastric veins and the gastro-omental veins of the stomach join along the way.

check.q: Which two veins join to form the hepatic portal vein?
check.a: The splenic vein and the superior mesenteric vein.

steps.title: Into the liver and out again
steps.text: The hepatic portal vein runs up to the liver, receiving the small cystic vein from the gallbladder, and branches within it down to the sinusoids. Processed blood collects in the central veins of the lobules, then in the hepatic veins, which open into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm.

check.q: How does blood leave the liver?
check.a: Through the hepatic veins into the inferior vena cava.

steps.title: Following a nutrient
steps.text: A glucose molecule absorbed in the jejunum enters a capillary of a villus, then an intestinal vein, the superior mesenteric vein and the hepatic portal vein. It crosses the liver sinusoids - where much of it may be stored as glycogen - then leaves through a central vein and a hepatic vein into the inferior vena cava and the right atrium.

check.q: Why does blood from the intestines pass through the liver first?
check.a: So absorbed nutrients can be processed and stored, and toxins and bacteria removed, before the blood reaches the general circulation.

practice.q: Trace blood from the small intestine to the right atrium
The inferior mesenteric vein usually drains into the:
practice.why: It joins the splenic vein behind the pancreas.

practice.q: Which vein drains the gallbladder?
practice.a: The cystic vein, into the hepatic portal system.

practice.q: What do Kupffer cells do?
practice.a: They are liver macrophages that remove bacteria, debris and old cells from the blood in the sinusoids.

title: Fetal circulation
summary: The placenta, the umbilical vessels and the three shunts that bypass the fetal liver and lungs.
objectives: Describe exchange at the placenta
Name the umbilical vessels and what each carries
Explain the ductus venosus, foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus and what each becomes after birth
takeaways: The fetus exchanges gases and nutrients at the placenta; its lungs are not yet in use.
One umbilical vein brings oxygenated blood; two umbilical arteries (from the internal iliacs) return it.
Ductus venosus (bypasses liver) → ligamentum venosum; foramen ovale (RA → LA) → fossa ovalis; ductus arteriosus (pulmonary trunk → aorta) → ligamentum arteriosum.
A foramen ovale that fails to close lets blood mix - a cause of a 'blue baby'.

steps.title: The placenta
steps.text:
Before birth the lungs are filled with fluid, so the placenta does their job. Fetal capillaries run in chorionic villi that dip into pools of maternal blood - the lacunae - fed by maternal arterioles and drained by venules in the endometrium.

Oxygen and nutrients cross from maternal to fetal blood; CO₂ and wastes cross back. The two bloods do not mix.

check.q: Where does the fetus get its oxygen?
check.a: From maternal blood across the placenta.

steps.title: The umbilical vessels
steps.text:
The umbilical cord carries three vessels. The single umbilical vein brings oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus. The two umbilical arteries, branches of the internal iliac arteries, carry deoxygenated blood back to the placenta.

After birth the vein becomes the round ligament of the liver and the arteries the medial umbilical ligaments.

check.q: Which umbilical vessel carries oxygenated blood?
check.a: The umbilical vein.

steps.title: Ductus venosus: bypassing the liver
steps.text:
Most umbilical-vein blood skips the liver through the ductus venosus, a channel straight into the inferior vena cava. The fetal liver needs only part of the flow, and oxygen-rich blood reaches the heart faster.

After birth the ductus closes and becomes the ligamentum venosum, which lies in a fissure on the underside of the liver.

check.q: What does the ductus venosus become after birth?
check.a: The ligamentum venosum.

steps.title: Foramen ovale: bypassing the lungs, part 1
steps.text:
In the right atrium much of the incoming blood passes straight through the foramen ovale, a flap-valve opening in the interatrial septum, into the left atrium, then the left ventricle and aorta - skipping the lungs.

At birth left atrial pressure rises and the flap is pushed shut, leaving the fossa ovalis. If it stays open (a patent foramen ovale), mixing can make a baby cyanotic - a 'blue baby'.

check.q: What is left of the foramen ovale in the adult heart?
check.a: The fossa ovalis.

steps.title: Ductus arteriosus: bypassing the lungs, part 2
steps.text:
Blood that does reach the right ventricle is pumped into the pulmonary trunk, but the collapsed lungs resist flow. Most of it crosses the ductus arteriosus, a short vessel from the pulmonary trunk to the aortic arch.

Within days of birth it closes to become the ligamentum arteriosum.

check.q: Which two vessels does the ductus arteriosus connect?
check.a: The pulmonary trunk and the aortic arch.

practice.q: The ductus venosus carries blood from the umbilical vein to the:
practice.why: It bypasses the liver into the IVC.

practice.q: The umbilical arteries arise from the:
practice.why: They branch from the internal iliacs.

practice.q: Which fetal structure becomes the ligamentum arteriosum?
practice.why: The ductus arteriosus closes after birth.

practice.q: A 'blue baby' can result from:
practice.why: Persistent shunting lets deoxygenated blood reach the systemic circulation.

practice.q: Trace oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetal aorta via the foramen ovale
Name the structures of the placental exchange surface.
practice.a: Chorionic villi containing fetal arterioles, capillaries and venules, bathed by maternal blood in lacunae fed by maternal arterioles and drained by venules of the endometrium.

practice.q: What does the umbilical vein become after birth?
practice.a: The round ligament of the liver (ligamentum teres).

title: Cat vessels compared with human
summary: How the arteries and veins of a dissected cat map onto human anatomy, and where they differ.
objectives: Describe how an injected specimen is coloured and name the body-cavity linings
List the main differences in arterial branching between cat and human
List the main venous differences and the organs found alongside
takeaways: Injected specimens: arteries red, veins blue, hepatic portal system yellow.
Cat aortic arch has two branches (brachiocephalic → both common carotids + right subclavian; left subclavian); human has three.
Cat has no common iliac artery: external iliacs, then internal iliacs + caudal artery.
Cat: no basilic vein, external jugular larger than internal, a caudal vein; names like internal mammary = internal thoracic.

steps.title: Injected specimens and body cavities
steps.text:
In preserved specimens the vessels are filled with coloured latex: arteries red, veins blue, and in a triple-injected specimen the hepatic portal system yellow.

The body cavity (coelom) is lined by parietal peritoneum, and the organs are covered by visceral peritoneum. The greater omentum hangs like an apron over the intestines, and the heart sits in its pericardial sac between the lungs.

check.q: What colour is the hepatic portal system in a triple-injected specimen?
check.a: Yellow.

steps.title: Arch, neck and axilla
steps.text: The cat's aortic arch has only two branches: a brachiocephalic artery giving both common carotids and the right subclavian, and the left subclavian. The subclavian gives vertebral, costocervical, thyrocervical and internal mammary (= internal thoracic) arteries; in the axilla the ventral thoracic and long thoracic arteries (≈ pectoral branches of the thoraco-acromial, and lateral thoracic) supply the pectorals and latissimus dorsi. The external maxillary artery is our facial artery.

check.q: How many branches does the cat's aortic arch have, compared with the human?
check.a: Two in the cat (brachiocephalic and left subclavian); three in the human.

steps.title: Abdomen and pelvis
steps.text: In the cat the aorta lies left and the caudal vena cava right. The coeliac artery and the cranial mesenteric (superior mesenteric) match ours; paired adrenolumbar arteries do the work of our suprarenal and lumbar arteries, and the posterior phrenic is our inferior phrenic. The cat has no common iliac: the aorta gives the external iliacs, then the internal iliacs, and continues as the caudal artery (our median sacral) into the tail.

check.q: Which human artery corresponds to the cat's caudal artery?
check.a: The median sacral artery.

steps.title: Veins of the upper body
steps.text: The cat has no basilic vein: radial and ulnar veins form the brachial vein, and the cephalic drains through the transverse scapular vein into the external jugular. Its external jugular is larger than the internal - the reverse of ours - and a transverse jugular vein links the two sides. Subscapular, thoracodorsal, long thoracic (lateral thoracic) and internal mammary (sternal) veins match the arteries, and the azygos lies on the right.

check.q: Which jugular vein is larger in the cat?
check.a: The external jugular vein.

steps.title: Veins of the abdomen and the organs alongside
steps.text: The cat's common iliacs join a caudal vein from the tail to form the caudal vena cava. As in us, the right gonadal vein enters the vena cava and the left the left renal vein; iliolumbar and adrenolumbar veins drain the wall. A gastrosplenic vein and the superior mesenteric form the portal vein. Nearby lie the kidneys, adrenals, the testes in the scrotum with the epididymis (or ovary and oviduct), and the ureter and ductus deferens crossing the external iliac vessels.

check.q: Which cat vein joins the common iliacs, and why do humans lack it?
check.a: The caudal vein from the tail - humans have no tail.

practice.q: In the cat, both common carotid arteries arise from the:
practice.why: The cat's brachiocephalic gives both carotids and the right subclavian.

practice.q: The cat's internal mammary artery is the human:
practice.why: Internal mammary = internal thoracic.

practice.q: Which vein does the cat lack?
practice.why: The cat has no basilic vein.

practice.q: Name the linings of the coelom.
practice.a: Parietal peritoneum lines the body wall; visceral peritoneum covers the organs.

practice.q: What is the cat's gastrosplenic vein?
practice.a: The vein draining stomach and spleen into the hepatic portal vein (≈ human splenic vein with gastric tributaries).
